peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What scent did Kostya notice in the ruined city?
options: Wet earth
Fresh coffee
Women’s perfume
Burnt rubber
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: the stench of burnt flesh, of smoke from the fires… and women’s perfume

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How were the mirrors positioned in Kostya’s hideout?
options: Beside the barricade, facing the stairwell
Across from the windows, facing the avenue
Above the door, angled toward the elevators
In the corners, angled to show both entrances
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Two mirrors, angled in the corners so that he could see both entrances without showing himself

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Which behavior helped Kostya recognize the girl as a lizard?
options: She had half-bent knees and a twitching head
She walked with a limp and avoided the light
She spoke in a voice that sounded mechanical
She kept rubbing her hands together
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: half-bent knees, a nervous twitch of the head

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What had the lizard who joined Kostya’s squad claimed about the dozen others she brought?
options: They were members of a nearby resistance group
They were former soldiers under her command
They were refugees from the city center
They were her relatives
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: brought a dozen more, saying they were her relatives

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Where was Kostya when the first Free Will broadcast aired?
options: Sheltering in an office tower
At a shooting competition
On patrol outside the city
At a government checkpoint
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Kostya was at a shooting competition at the time and missed the broadcast entirely.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: According to Free Will’s second broadcast, what did the invaders feed on by taking over human bodies?
options: Human memories, dreams, and physical strength
Human consciousness, emotion, and life-force
Human blood, bones, and body heat
Human speech, movement, and sensory energy
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: they fed on human consciousness, emotion, and life-force.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How long did the riots following Free Will’s second broadcast rage?
options: One day
A week
Three days
Two days
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Riots erupted in all major cities and raged for two days.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What did Free Will say could reveal an alien disguised as a human?
options: An unusual accent that could not be concealed
A refusal to use weapons or enter buildings
Odd behavior when the true face slipped through
A mark on the skin that appeared in sunlight
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Their alien nature made it impossible for them to act human all the time; now and then their true face slipped through the mask.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How many disguised aliens did Kostya say he had shot by that point?
options: Two dozen
A dozen
Six
Eight
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Kostya himself had shot a dozen disguised aliens by now

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What did Taka report about Earth’s population and surface?
options: The population had fallen tenfold, and two-thirds of the surface was uninhabitable
The population had doubled, but two-thirds of the surface was uninhabitable
The population had halved, and one-third of the surface was uninhabitable
The population had fallen tenfold, and half the surface was uninhabitable
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: The planet’s population has decreased tenfold. Its energy system is destroyed. After the use of the most powerful weapons, two-thirds of the surface is uninhabitable.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What was the sik used for?
options: Recording visual images of a planet’s inhabitants
Sending telepathic messages between ships
Measuring a planet’s energy systems from orbit
Storing data encoded in a specially bred bacterium’s DNA
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: a small cylindrical object used for data storage — a sik. Inside, encoded in the DNA of a specially bred bacterium

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How many new symbols did Taka hope to earn for his name?
options: One
Ten
Two
Three
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: it could earn him three new symbols for his name.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What did Thorg say when Taka asked to record new data onto the sik?
options: “Do it before we leave orbit.”
“Later. I want to review the material once more.”
“Give the sik to me and return to your station.”
“The Council must approve it first.”
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: ‘Later. I want to review the material once more.’

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How did the Council learn about the events involving Taka and Thorg?
options: From a report delivered by the rescue team’s captain
From a recording stored in the damaged scout’s navigation system
From a message Taka sent before boarding the scout ship
From a translated visual recording made by an aboriginal of the destroyed planet
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Most of our information comes from a translated visual recording by one of the aboriginals of the destroyed planet.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What fell from the sky as Kostya headed toward the distant gunfire?
options: Rain
Snow
Soot
Ash
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: From the sky, large flakes of snow began to fall.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Why does Free Will’s series of broadcasts lead to the collapse of human society?
options: Each broadcast causes people to unite behind the governments and attack the resistance
Each broadcast persuades people to abandon cities and stop maintaining power systems
Each broadcast convinces the military to surrender Earth to the aliens
Each broadcast intensifies suspicion until people turn against governments, soldiers, and one another
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: The result was full-scale civil war in every country.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Why does the aliens’ method of conquest work especially well on an industrial world?
options: It persuades the inhabitants to build ships that carry the invaders to other planets
It disables advanced weapons before the inhabitants can learn of the invasion
It uses the world’s information networks to provoke its inhabitants into destroying themselves
It takes advantage of industrial workers’ dependence on alien technology
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: A bit of study, a carefully crafted provocation, and the natives would annihilate themselves.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What is the main irony in the Council’s interpretation of Taka’s actions?
options: The Council sees Taka as infected by an invader, although he had devised the conquest plan himself
The Council thinks Thorg survived, although Taka had killed him in the ship’s chamber
The Council believes Earth is untouched, although it has already begun to colonize the planet
The Council suspects the rescue team, although its members had sent the scout to Earth
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: The younger, named Taka, was infected by the parasitic organism and attacked the elder, Thorg.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does Thorg’s ambition shape his response to Taka’s discovery?
options: He rejects the discovery because he wants the Council to resume costly military campaigns
He plans to take credit for the discovery and eliminate Taka so he can rise in the Council
He protects Taka because he believes the younger scout can lead the colonization
He plans to share the discovery with Taka so they can rule the Council together
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: The death of insignificant Taka would go unnoticed.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Why does Taka reach for the blaster after Thorg postpones his request?
options: He suspects Thorg has already been infected by an organism from Earth
He thinks Thorg is about to destroy the sik and erase the conquest plan
He realizes Thorg intends to keep the research and prevent Taka from benefiting from it
He wants to warn the Council that the ship’s orbit has become unsafe
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Now there was no doubt — Thorg would never let his research leave his claws.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does the contrast between Kostya’s view and the Council’s view reveal?
options: Kostya understands the alien plan, while the Council remains unaware of any invasion
The Council trusts its citizens, while Kostya relies only on official reports
Both sides interpret unfamiliar behavior as evidence of an alien threat, and each risks acting on a mistaken account
Both sides know that the other is deliberately spreading accurate information
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Members of the Council of Aggressors looked around at one another with suspicion — as though seeing each other for the first time.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What role does Kostya’s shooting practice play in the ending?
options: It shows that his former squad had trained him to identify aliens by sight
It connects a seemingly pointless past habit to his immediate survival in the ruined world
It explains why he was away when the first broadcast began the civil war
It proves that he can defeat the invaders without help from his people
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: So there was the answer to his wife’s old question: What good is all that stupid shooting practice?

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does the recurring idea of disguised invaders connect the human and alien storylines?
options: Both groups confidently identify infiltrators by the same physical signs
Humans hunt supposed infiltrators, while the Council later fears that its own society is being infiltrated
The human resistance and the Council cooperate to expose the same invaders
The Council teaches Kostya how to recognize aliens through telepathy
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: there are more reports of strange behavior among our citizens.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does the falling snow in July most strongly suggest about Earth’s condition?
options: The aliens have used a device to cover the planet in protective snow
The nuclear winter has altered the climate, confirming the devastation caused by the war
A natural seasonal change has begun, giving the survivors a reason to leave the city
The damaged power grid has caused a temporary storm over Kostya’s district
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: the nuclear winter had begun.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What is the effect of placing the Council’s scene between the devastation of Earth and Kostya’s final actions?
options: It explains that Earth’s war was staged by the Council to test its military
It shows that the Council has already rescued Kostya and his remaining people
It reveals that the conflict’s consequences may spread beyond Earth, then returns to one survivor’s struggle
It resolves the invasion by showing that both planets have agreed to peace
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: For the first time in our history, we are the victims of aggression rather than the aggressors.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does the text suggest about information withheld by authorities and information spread without scrutiny?
options: Both secrecy and unverified claims can leave people vulnerable to manipulation and violence
Only government secrecy is dangerous; public claims reliably protect people
Information matters less than military strength in determining who survives
Open information prevents conflict because people can always verify its source
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Fortunately, the guys from Free Will didn’t hoard information the way the world’s governments did.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Why is the perfume detail significant beyond simply identifying the girl’s presence?
options: It shows that Kostya’s hideout is still connected to the office building’s ventilation
It reveals that the girl is trying to attract Kostya rather than attack him
It hints at a remnant of ordinary human life, while Kostya interprets it through his hard-earned suspicion
It proves that the girl has recently arrived from a clean and safe shelter
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: or perhaps it was her final link to the past.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does Taka’s ambition differ from Thorg’s, even though both seek advancement?
options: Taka wants recognition for his own discovery, while Thorg plans to claim its benefits and discard him
Taka seeks personal wealth, while Thorg is motivated only by concern for Earth
Taka wants to preserve the old military order, while Thorg wants to end all conquest
Taka wants to join the Council through service, while Thorg wants to leave it behind
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Takargkh — it had a fine ring to it, a leader’s name, not that of a minor scout aboard a reconnaissance ship.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does the ending’s “life went on” idea emphasize?
options: The nuclear winter is harmless and ordinary life will soon return to normal
The surviving resistance has already defeated the aliens and restored order
Kostya believes the war has ended and no longer expects to find his people
Even amid catastrophe, Kostya continues toward a practical goal rather than giving up
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: But life went on. He had to find his people and fight the enemy.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does the story’s shift from Kostya’s perspective to the alien ship change the reader’s understanding of the human war?
options: It reveals that the war was not merely resistance to an invasion but a deliberate means of making Earth easy to seize
It proves that Kostya’s group had secretly been working for the alien Council
It explains that the human conflict began only after the aliens launched a direct attack
It shows that the aliens abandoned their plan when Earth’s power grids failed
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Now they could seize advanced planets with almost no expense.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What parallel links the final warning from Free Will with the Council Chairman’s warning?
options: Both identify the same individual as the source of the invasion
Both announce that the invasion has ended and peace has been restored
Both urge vigilance against infiltration, but the warnings also fuel suspicion within their societies
Both instruct citizens to trust military leaders and avoid forming militias
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: We must remain vigilant — the recording warns that the first to be infected are government officials and military personnel.

the-nose.question: What was written on Ivan Jakovlevitch’s sign-board?
options: Shaving done here.
Razors sharpened here.
Blood-letting done here.
Coffee and bread served here.
the-nose.evidence: "Blood-letting done here."

the-nose.question: What did Ivan Jakovlevitch say he wanted for breakfast?
options: A fresh loaf with butter.
A glass of punch with bread.
A cup of coffee with cream.
A fresh loaf with onions.
the-nose.evidence: "I should like a fresh loaf with onions."

the-nose.question: Which days did Ivan Jakovlevitch shave Kovaloff?
options: Every Friday and Sunday.
Every Tuesday and Saturday.
Every Monday and Thursday.
Every Sunday and Wednesday.
the-nose.evidence: "whom he shaved every Sunday and Wednesday."

the-nose.question: What did the sentry say when Ivan Jakovlevitch let the wrapped nose drop?
options: Come back! You have dropped your parcel!
Look out! You have let something drop!
Stop there! You have lost your way!
Move along! You are blocking the bridge!
the-nose.evidence: "Look out! You have let something drop!"

the-nose.question: Where did Ivan Jakovlevitch finally throw the nose?
options: Into a canal from the Ascension Bridge.
Into a public square near the police station.
Into the Neva from the Isaac Bridge.
Into a drain beside the advertisement office.
the-nose.evidence: "secretly threw the nose, wrapped in a little piece of cloth, into the water."

the-nose.question: What position had Kovaloff come to St Petersburg hoping to obtain?
options: Police commissary of a district.
Vice-governor of a province.
Director of the Academy of Surgery.
Inspector of the city advertisement office.
the-nose.evidence: "if possible that of vice-governor of a province"

the-nose.question: What was engraved on some of Kovaloff’s seals?
options: The names of his Caucasian colleagues.
The dates of his visits to the theatre.
The titles of his hoped-for positions.
The names of the days of the week.
the-nose.evidence: "others the names of the days of the week."

the-nose.question: What rank did the nose’s plume-adorned uniform indicate?
options: Police inspector.
State-councillor.
Vice-governor.
Major.
the-nose.evidence: "The hat, adorned with a plume, showed that it held the rank of a state-councillor."

the-nose.question: Where did the carriage carrying the nose stop?
options: Before the Grand Bazar of Moscow.
Outside the police superintendent’s house.
In front of the Northern Bee office.
At the entrance to the Isaac Bridge.
the-nose.evidence: "stopped a short way off before the Grand Bazar of Moscow."

the-nose.question: What had the earlier advertisement for a lost poodle supposedly meant?
options: A satire about a cashier.
A complaint about a careless barber.
A notice about a missing clerk.
A joke about a countess’s dog.
the-nose.evidence: "by the poodle was meant the cashier of some establishment or other."

the-nose.question: Why did Kovaloff reject the official’s offer of snuff?
options: He lacked the essential feature for taking it.
He disliked the portrait on the snuff-box lid.
He believed the snuff would make his face swell.
He had already taken too much snuff that morning.
the-nose.evidence: "I lack precisely the essential feature for taking snuff?"

the-nose.question: Where was the nose supposedly going when the police official arrested it?
options: The Tauris Gardens.
Riga.
Moscow.
The Caucasus.
the-nose.evidence: "It has been arrested just as it was getting into a carriage for Riga."

the-nose.question: What mixture did the doctor suggest for preserving the nose?
options: Brandy mixed with two spoonfuls of vinegar.
Cold water mixed with a spoonful of snuff.
Spirits mixed with fresh apple juice.
Warm vinegar mixed with two spoonfuls of brandy.
the-nose.evidence: "of warm vinegar mixed with two spoonfuls of brandy"

the-nose.question: Where did one rumour place the nose instead of on the Neffsky Avenue?
options: The Tauris Gardens.
Junker’s stores.
The Isaac Bridge.
The Ascension Bridge.
the-nose.evidence: "the nose of Major Kovaloff was in the habit of walking not on the Neffsky Avenue but in the Tauris Gardens."

the-nose.question: How did Ivan Jakovlevitch manage to shave Kovaloff after the nose returned?
options: He used a cloth to cover the nose while shaving.
He braced his thumb against Kovaloff’s lower jaw and cheek.
He held Kovaloff’s chin with both hands throughout the shave.
He shaved only the side of Kovaloff’s face.
the-nose.evidence: "placing his wrinkled thumb against the Major's lower jaw and cheek"

the-nose.question: Why is Ivan Jakovlevitch so anxious to get rid of the nose?
options: He fears the police will treat him as responsible for its disappearance.
He believes it will bring bad luck to his shop.
He hopes to sell it to the doctor for a good price.
He wants to hide it from Kovaloff’s wife and family.
the-nose.evidence: "The thought that the police might find him in unlawful possession of a nose and arrest him"

the-nose.question: What does Prasskovna Ossipovna’s reaction to the nose mainly reveal about her?
options: She suspects the nose belongs to her and wants to keep it.
She believes Ivan should take the nose directly to a doctor.
She is frightened that Kovaloff will stop being her customer.
She is more concerned with blame and avoiding trouble than helping Ivan.
the-nose.evidence: "Am I to undertake all responsibility for you at the police-office?"

the-nose.question: What does Kovaloff’s encounter with the nose reveal about the importance he places on rank?
options: He thinks the nose’s uniform proves that it has been appointed to his post.
He assumes that a state-councillor must obey anyone with a military title.
He expects the nose’s social status to determine how it should behave toward him.
He decides that rank no longer matters once the nose has left his face.
the-nose.evidence: "To judge by the buttons of your uniform, you must be in quite a different department to mine."

the-nose.question: Why is losing his nose especially distressing to Kovaloff?
options: He fears it will damage his appearance and his prospects in society.
He thinks he will be unable to recognize his friends.
He believes he can no longer perform his duties as a barber.
He worries that the police will dismiss him from his current post.
the-nose.evidence: "I go into good society, and this evening I am invited to two parties."

the-nose.question: Why does the advertisement official refuse to print Kovaloff’s notice at first?
options: He says the paper only prints advertisements from government officials.
He believes Kovaloff has not offered enough money for the notice.
He assumes the nose belongs to a noblewoman’s missing dog.
He thinks an advertisement about a lost nose would make the paper seem unreliable.
the-nose.evidence: "Because it might compromise the paper."

the-nose.question: What does the police commissary’s conversation about cheques suggest about his character?
options: He is chiefly concerned with the comfort of his mother-in-law.
He is cautious because he fears being accused of theft.
He is devoted to solving unusual cases without payment.
He is self-interested and especially attracted to financial gain.
the-nose.evidence: "what he liked above everything else was a cheque."

the-nose.question: Why does Kovaloff suspect Madame Podtotchina of causing his misfortune?
options: He connects it to her wish that he marry her daughter and his refusal to commit.
He believes she arranged for the barber to steal his nose during a shave.
He thinks she has been secretly trying to obtain his government position.
He assumes she wants to sell his nose to the doctor.
the-nose.evidence: "This must be the reason why the lady, in revenge, had resolved to bring him into disgrace"

the-nose.question: What does Madame Podtotchina’s reply lead Kovaloff to conclude?
options: She has mistaken Kovaloff for another official.
Her letter seems too sincere for her to be guilty.
She is willing to return the nose if he pays her.
She admits that she used magic to remove his nose.
the-nose.evidence: "Such a letter could not be written by a criminal."

the-nose.question: What is the effect of the city’s rumours about the walking nose?
options: They help Kovaloff discover the nose’s exact location and recover it.
They turn an extraordinary private misfortune into public entertainment and spectacle.
They convince the public that Kovaloff has committed a crime.
They persuade the authorities to close the advertisement office.
the-nose.evidence: "The crowd of curious spectators which gathered there daily was enormous."

the-nose.question: What does the doctor’s advice to preserve and sell the nose contribute to the story?
options: It proves that the doctor knows who caused the nose to disappear.
It persuades Kovaloff that life without a nose will improve his health.
It offers a reliable way to attach the nose back to Kovaloff’s face.
It treats an impossible event with absurdly practical, commercial reasoning.
the-nose.evidence: "I advise you to have it preserved in a bottle of spirits"

the-nose.question: Why does the nose’s recovery fail to solve Kovaloff’s problem immediately?
options: He cannot make it stay attached to his face.
The police will not release it from their custody.
Kovaloff discovers that it belongs to someone else.
The doctor says it has been damaged beyond recognition.
the-nose.evidence: "however often he tried, all his efforts were in vain."

the-nose.question: What is emphasized by the nose returning to its proper place without explanation?
options: Ivan Jakovlevitch has finally confessed to cutting it off.
Kovaloff’s accusation against Madame Podtotchina is secretly confirmed.
The story refuses to provide a rational cause or orderly resolution for the bizarre event.
The police have discovered a medical treatment that restores it.
the-nose.evidence: "The same nose ... was found one morning in its proper place"

the-nose.question: What does Kovaloff’s behaviour after the nose returns suggest about his character?
options: He decides to dedicate himself to helping people with similar misfortunes.
He quickly resumes his old social ambitions and attention to pretty women.
He gives up his hopes of marrying and seeking a position.
He becomes ashamed of his vanity and avoids public life.
the-nose.evidence: "the Major resumed his walks on the Neffsky Avenue and his visits to the theatre as if nothing had happened."

the-nose.question: How does the narrator’s closing reflection shape the reader’s understanding of the story?
options: It acknowledges the tale’s improbability while insisting that rare strange events do happen.
It concludes that the nose’s disappearance was a deliberate political plot.
It reveals that the story was invented to warn against drinking too much.
It explains that the whole incident was only Kovaloff’s dream.
the-nose.evidence: "such cases do occur--rarely, it is true, but now and then actually."

As landmarks for finding the old village

The siege of Fort Christina

He helped them build stone fences

He made playthings and taught them games

It broke through the fence into a neighbour’s field
It refused to come in when the rain began
It wandered into the woods after squirrels

A blue mountain beneath a crown of clouds
A portrait of Peter Stuyvesant
A Dutch ship on the Hudson

He nodded after slowly inhaling and emitting smoke
He tapped his pipe against the bench

rip-van-winkle.question: What was Rip doing when he climbed high into the Kaatskill Mountains?
options: Searching for his missing cow
Looking for a lost village child
Following a mountain stream
Squirrel shooting

rip-van-winkle.question: What was the stranger carrying when Rip first saw him?

A keg that seemed full of liquor
A bundle of firewood tied with vines
A long fowling-piece wrapped in cloth

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Rip think the drink tasted like?
options: Sweet cider from the village
A strong Dutch beer
A bitter mountain herb brew
Excellent Hollands

options: It was still there but soaked by the stream
It had been replaced by a rusty old firelock
It had been broken into several pieces
It was missing, but its strap lay beside him

rip-van-winkle.question: What name was painted over the door of the new hotel?
options: The Hudson House, by Peter Vanderdonk
The Union Hotel, by Jonathan Doolittle
The King’s Arms, by Nicholas Vedder
The Washington Inn, by Brom Dutcher

A fit of passion at a New-England pedler
A fever that followed a storm
A fall on the road to the village

options: Every ten years
Every twenty years
Whenever a thunderstorm came
Every summer afternoon

rip-van-winkle.question: In the postscript’s Indian legend, what happened after the hunter dropped a gourd among the rocks?
options: A bear chased him down to the Hudson
A stream burst forth and swept him away
The gourd changed into a cluster of stars
A storm cloud covered the Garden Rock
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he let it fall among the rocks, when a great stream gushed forth

rip-van-winkle.question: What contrast does the story draw between Rip’s willingness to work and his attitude toward his own farm?
options: He tends his farm carefully but refuses to help anyone else
He avoids all hard work, whether for himself or others
He works only when his wife praises his efforts
He works diligently for neighbours but neglects his own affairs
rip-van-winkle.evidence: Rip was ready to attend to anybody’s business but his own

rip-van-winkle.question: Why does Rip so often leave the house and wander outdoors?
options: He wants to escape his wife’s scolding and the demands of the farm
He is trying to persuade Wolf to become a hunting dog
He is searching for a political cause to support
He hopes to find a more profitable farm beyond the village
rip-van-winkle.evidence: his only alternative, to escape from the labour of the farm and clamour of his wife, was to take gun in hand and stroll away into the woods

rip-van-winkle.question: What does Rip’s relationship with Wolf show about their shared life at home?
options: Both are afraid of strangers but brave around Dame Van Winkle
Both are treated as companions in idleness and suffer under Dame Van Winkle’s temper
Both secretly help Dame Van Winkle keep the farm in order
Both prefer the village inn to wandering in the woods
rip-van-winkle.evidence: Dame Van Winkle regarded them as companions in idleness

rip-van-winkle.question: How does the village gathering place help emphasize the change Rip encounters after waking?
options: The inn has become a farm, showing that village life has ended
The village has become quieter because its residents have moved away
The old sages have returned, but now argue about mountain legends
The quiet inn and its passive company have given way to a busy, political crowd
rip-van-winkle.evidence: There was a busy, bustling, disputatious tone about it, instead of the accustomed phlegm and drowsy tranquillity

rip-van-winkle.question: Why does Rip’s encounter with the strange mountain company lead to his long absence?
options: He loses his way while searching for his dog
He is taken prisoner after refusing to serve their commander
He joins their game and chooses to remain in the mountains
He drinks repeatedly from their flagon and falls into a deep sleep
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he reiterated his visits to the flagon so often that at length his senses were overpowered

rip-van-winkle.question: What is the main effect of Rip’s return to a village that seems familiar in its setting but strange in its people and buildings?
options: It convinces him that the mountain drink has made him unable to see
It reveals that an extraordinary span of time has passed while he slept
It makes him realize that he has crossed into a different country
It shows that his neighbours have deliberately changed the village to trick him
rip-van-winkle.evidence: the whole twenty years had seemed to him as but one night

rip-van-winkle.question: What does the transformation of the inn’s sign from George the Third to General Washington help demonstrate?
options: Rip has returned to the village during a war with the Dutch
The villagers have abandoned politics in favour of the old monarchy
The innkeeper has changed his allegiance but the village has not
The village has changed from British rule to an independent United States
rip-van-winkle.evidence: instead of being a subject of his Majesty George the Third, he was now a free citizen of the United States

rip-van-winkle.question: How does Rip respond to the political changes that have taken place during his sleep?
options: He is confused by the changes and largely uninterested in politics
He eagerly takes sides in the new political debates
He regrets that the village no longer supports the king
He decides to campaign for a place in Congress
rip-van-winkle.evidence: Rip, in fact, was no politician; the changes of states and empires made but little impression on him

rip-van-winkle.question: Why does Rip feel some comfort when he learns that Dame Van Winkle has died?
options: He believes she left him the farm in good condition
He no longer has to fear the domestic authority that had troubled him
He hopes she can explain what happened on the mountain
He thinks her death will restore his former friends to the village
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he had got his neck out of the yoke of matrimony

rip-van-winkle.question: What does the fate of Rip’s son suggest about the habits passed between generations?
options: His son repeats Rip’s tendency to neglect his own work
His son becomes a diligent farmer unlike his father
His son takes over the inn and becomes a politician
His son abandons the village to join the army
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he evinced an hereditary disposition to attend to anything else but his business

rip-van-winkle.question: How does living with Judith allow Rip to resume his old habits?
options: She expects him to manage the farm that her husband has neglected
Her comfortable household leaves him free from the duties of running his own home
She sends him back to the mountains to recover his old gun
She asks him to teach the village children and run errands
rip-van-winkle.evidence: Rip’s daughter took him home to live with her; she had a snug, well-furnished house

rip-van-winkle.question: What role does Peter Vanderdonk play after Rip tells his story?
options: He uses local tradition to support the possibility of Rip’s account
He claims that Rip’s story belongs to an old German superstition
He disputes Rip’s account and says the mountain is ordinary
He identifies the strange men as soldiers from the Revolutionary War
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he corroborated his story in the most satisfactory manner

rip-van-winkle.question: What does the recurring wish of hen-pecked husbands for a draught from Rip’s flagon suggest about the ending?
options: The husbands want to join Hudson’s crew at ninepins
The husbands hope to become wealthy through mountain adventures
The flagon represents an escape from burdensome domestic life
The flagon is a cure for the physical effects of old age
rip-van-winkle.evidence: it is a common wish of all hen-pecked husbands in the neighbourhood, when life hangs heavy on their hands, that they might have a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle’s flagon

rip-van-winkle.question: What is the effect of the narrator’s note insisting that Rip’s story is beyond doubt?
options: It proves that the narrator witnessed the mountain game himself
It presents the tale with mock-serious evidence while preserving its fantastic character
It rejects local traditions in favour of a German explanation
It explains that Rip invented his story to avoid paying his debts
rip-van-winkle.evidence: The story, therefore, is beyond the possibility of doubt.

rip-van-winkle.question: How does the postscript’s account of the Catskill spirits relate to the tale of Rip?
options: It shows that Rip’s family descended from the spirits of the Catskills
It places the strange events in a region already associated with supernatural beings
It explains that the villagers built the mountains to hide the inn
It establishes that the mountain spirits were created by the Revolutionary War
rip-van-winkle.evidence: The Kaatsberg or Catskill mountains have always been a region full of fable.

rip-van-winkle.question: What does Rip’s return to the bench at the inn show about how he fits into the changed village?
options: He takes charge of the village’s political meetings
He tries to restore the old inn and its Dutch sign
He becomes a respected link to the village’s earlier days
He gives up his easygoing ways and becomes a farmer
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he was reverenced as one of the patriarchs of the village, and a chronicle of the old times “before the war.”

rip-van-winkle.question: How does the story connect Rip’s personal liberation with the larger political change in the village?
options: He is largely indifferent to national independence but glad to escape his wife’s rule
He leaves his daughter’s home to fight for the new republic
He welcomes the revolution because it gives him a role in government
He believes the war began because of Dame Van Winkle’s temper
rip-van-winkle.evidence: there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was--petticoat government.

a-christmas-carol.question: Who signed the register of Jacob Marley's burial?
options: The clergyman, the clerk, the undertaker, and the chief mourner
The clerk, Scrooge, the gravedigger, and the chief mourner
The undertaker, two partners, the clerk, and Marley's sister
The clergyman, the doctor, the undertaker, and Scrooge's nephew
a-christmas-carol.evidence: The register of his burial was signed by the clergyman, the clerk, the undertaker, and the chief mourner.

a-christmas-carol.question: Where did Scrooge keep the coal-box used by his clerk?
options: Beside the counting-house door
In the clerk's little cell
In a cupboard near the stairs
In Scrooge's own room
a-christmas-carol.evidence: Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room

a-christmas-carol.question: What reason did Scrooge's nephew give for getting married?
options: He had fallen in love
He hoped to improve his social standing
He had promised his family he would
He wanted to share his good fortune
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Because I fell in love.”

a-christmas-carol.question: What did Scrooge say when the gentlemen asked what he would give to help the poor?
options: He would donate after the holidays
He would support the workhouses instead
He would give a small amount anonymously
He would give nothing and wished to be left alone
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Nothing!” Scrooge replied.

a-christmas-carol.question: Which objects were among the items making up Marley's chain?
options: Letters, scales, weights, tools, bottles, and iron bars
Deeds, candles, chairs, ropes, account books, and chains
Cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses
Coins, watches, rings, books, locks, and silver goblets
a-christmas-carol.evidence: it was made (for Scrooge observed it closely) of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel.

a-christmas-carol.question: What did the Ghost of Christmas Past carry in its hand?
options: A small candle in a brass holder
A flowering branch of winter berries
A branch of fresh green holly
A sprig of mistletoe
a-christmas-carol.evidence: It held a branch of fresh green holly in its hand

a-christmas-carol.question: Which storybook character did Scrooge recognize in the scene at his old school?
options: Valentine
Ali Baba
Robinson Crusoe
Orson
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Why, it's Ali Baba!” Scrooge exclaimed in ecstasy.

a-christmas-carol.question: What news did Fan bring her brother at the school?
options: Their mother had arranged for him to attend another school
Their uncle had promised to take him into business
Their father had sent for him to return home for good
Their father had agreed to visit him at Christmas
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “I have come to bring you home, dear brother!”

a-christmas-carol.question: Who was Scrooge's fellow apprentice at Fezziwig's warehouse?
options: Topper
Dick Wilkins
Peter Cratchit
Fred Scrooge
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Dick Wilkins, to be sure!” said Scrooge to the Ghost.

a-christmas-carol.question: What did Tiny Tim say after the Cratchit family toasted Christmas?
options: “God bless my father and mother!”
“God bless us every one!”
“May we all be together next year!”
“A Merry Christmas to us all!”
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all.

a-christmas-carol.question: What were the two children called whom the Ghost of Christmas Present revealed?
options: Hunger and Fear
Need and Despair
Poverty and Misery
Want and Ignorance
a-christmas-carol.evidence: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.

a-christmas-carol.question: What was the name of the shopkeeper who appraised the stolen goods in the rag-and-bone shop?
options: Mr. Dilber
Jacob Marley
Old Joe
The undertaker
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “You couldn't have met in a better place,” said old Joe

a-christmas-carol.question: What had the woman taken from the dead man's bed?
options: The coverlet and the bedside table
The sheets, pillows, and bedstead
The bed-curtains, rings and all
The mattress and all its blankets
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Bed-curtains!”

a-christmas-carol.question: What did Scrooge order the boy to buy on Christmas morning?
options: A basket of fruit for his nephew's family
A large prize turkey from the poulterer's
A goose and a plum pudding for the Cratchits
A roast of beef for the poorhouse
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Go and buy it.”

a-christmas-carol.question: How late was Bob Cratchit when he arrived at work the next morning?
options: A quarter of an hour
Twenty minutes exactly
Eighteen minutes and a half
Half an hour
a-christmas-carol.evidence: He was full eighteen minutes and a half behind his time.

a-christmas-carol.question: What purpose does the preface say the book's “Ghost of an Idea” is meant to serve?
options: To persuade readers to abandon Christmas celebrations
To make readers feel ashamed of their past behavior
To unsettle readers until they question their beliefs
To haunt readers pleasantly without making them dislike themselves or others
a-christmas-carol.evidence: May it haunt their houses pleasantly, and no one wish to lay it.

a-christmas-carol.question: Why does the narrator insist so firmly that Marley was dead before telling of his ghost?
options: To show that Scrooge had been unaware of Marley's death
To suggest that the burial records were inaccurate
To explain why Marley left his business to Scrooge
To establish that the ghost's appearance is genuinely extraordinary
a-christmas-carol.evidence: This must be distinctly understood, or nothing wonderful can come of the story I am going to relate.

a-christmas-carol.question: What most closely explains Scrooge's lack of human connection at the beginning?
options: He is too poor to take part in social life
He deliberately keeps sympathy and companionship at a distance
He believes his business partners have betrayed him
He has been rejected by everyone despite trying to be kind
a-christmas-carol.evidence: To edge his way along the crowded paths of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance, was what the knowing ones call “nuts” to Scrooge.

a-christmas-carol.question: How does Fred's response to Scrooge reveal an important contrast between them?
options: Fred responds to Scrooge's insults by demanding an apology
Fred answers Scrooge's hostility with persistent warmth and forgiveness
Fred avoids Scrooge because he disapproves of his business
Fred tries to outdo Scrooge's wealth through public generosity
a-christmas-carol.evidence: His nephew left the room without an angry word, notwithstanding.

a-christmas-carol.question: What does Scrooge's response to the charity collectors reveal about his view of poverty?
options: He believes personal generosity is more effective than public aid
He treats institutions and economic arguments as reasons not to help individuals
He thinks the poor should be helped only during winter
He worries that charity will make poor people dependent on him
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “It's not my business,” Scrooge returned.

a-christmas-carol.question: What does the chain Marley forged in life represent?
options: The ties of family that prevent a person from changing
The lasting burden of choices made through selfishness and neglect of others
The punishment for failing to protect one's business partners
The wealth that a person leaves behind after death
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “I wear the chain I forged in life,” replied the Ghost.

a-christmas-carol.question: Why does Marley arrange for three Spirits to visit Scrooge?
options: To help Scrooge understand his past, present, and possible future so he can escape Marley's fate
To make Scrooge repay the money Marley lost in business
To teach Scrooge how to manage his affairs after death
To prove that Scrooge's dreams are caused by illness
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate.”

a-christmas-carol.question: How does Scrooge's childhood at school help explain his later character?
options: His joyful school years make him resent Christmas as an adult
His strict education teaches him to value money above friendship
His father's early kindness convinces him that people need no help
His loneliness helps reveal the pain beneath his hardened, isolated manner
a-christmas-carol.evidence: Scrooge sat down upon a form, and wept to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be.

a-christmas-carol.question: What does Belle's decision to release Scrooge show about the change in their relationship?
options: She wants him to leave their town and seek a different career
She thinks he has become too poor to support a family
She has fallen in love with someone who is already wealthy
She believes his growing devotion to wealth has displaced his love for her
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “Another idol has displaced me”

a-christmas-carol.question: What lesson does Scrooge draw from Fezziwig's treatment of his employees?
options: A successful employer should spend little on celebrations
Workers are happiest when they are given expensive gifts
A business owner should keep friendship separate from work
A master can greatly affect workers' happiness through small acts of kindness
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune.”

a-christmas-carol.question: Why is the Cratchit family's Christmas dinner important to Scrooge's developing understanding?
options: It convinces him that the family is wealthy enough without his help
It shows him that affection and gratitude can thrive even amid hardship
It teaches him that Christmas matters only to children
It makes him believe that poverty is always a source of happiness
a-christmas-carol.evidence: they were happy, grateful, pleased with one another, and contented with the time

a-christmas-carol.question: What is the significance of the children named Ignorance and Want?
options: They are the Spirit's own children and will inherit his duties
They embody social problems that people neglect at their peril
They symbolize the childhood memories Scrooge has tried to forget
They represent the dangers of celebrating Christmas too freely
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.”

a-christmas-carol.question: What does Fred's attitude toward Scrooge suggest about the possibility of changing him?
options: Scrooge can change only if his family threatens to disown him
Scrooge's character is fixed, so Fred's invitations are merely polite
Fred believes Scrooge will become generous only after losing his wealth
Steady kindness may keep open a path to connection even when it is rejected
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “I mean to give him the same chance every year, whether he likes it or not, for I pity him.”

a-christmas-carol.question: Why do the people in the future scenes react so casually to the dead man's death?
options: His life has left him without affection or anyone who feels his loss
They have all been promised a share of his fortune
They do not know that he was once a successful businessman
They are frightened that the dead man will return as a ghost
a-christmas-carol.evidence: there was not a man, a woman, or a child, to say that he was kind to me in this or that

a-christmas-carol.question: What does the contrast between the dead man's lonely room and the Cratchits' grief suggest?
options: A person's reputation depends mainly on how much money they leave
Being loved and remembered matters more than wealth or social standing
Grief is appropriate only when the deceased was financially generous
Families should avoid showing sadness in front of children
a-christmas-carol.evidence: The only emotion that the Ghost could show him, caused by the event, was one of pleasure.

a-christmas-carol.question: What does Scrooge's reaction to seeing his own name on the grave demonstrate?
options: He believes the grave belongs to Marley rather than himself
He understands that his future is not inevitable if he changes how he lives
He decides that the Spirits have shown him a past event by mistake
He accepts that wealth is more valuable than other people's affection
a-christmas-carol.evidence: “But if the courses be departed from, the ends will change.”

a-christmas-carol.question: How does the ending connect Scrooge's changed outlook to the book's larger message?
options: He gives away his fortune once and then returns to his old habits
He turns his new understanding into lasting generosity and care for others
He learns that kindness matters only during the Christmas season
He avoids his former acquaintances and keeps his change private
a-christmas-carol.evidence: He had no further intercourse with Spirits, but lived upon the Total Abstinence Principle, ever afterwards

the-time-machine.question: What did the Time Traveller say about the chairs in his dining room?
options: They were borrowed from the Provincial Mayor for the evening.
They were made of ivory and crystalline substance.
They were arranged around a small table beside the fire.
They were his patents and seemed to embrace and caress their sitters.
the-time-machine.evidence: Our chairs, being his patents, embraced and caressed us

the-time-machine.question: How is Filby described when he first objects to the Time Traveller’s argument?
options: As a provincial official with knitted brows.
As a quiet, shy man with a beard.
As an argumentative person with red hair.
As a very young man trying to relight his cigar.
the-time-machine.evidence: said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

the-time-machine.question: What did the Time Traveller use as an example of a line traced along the Time-Dimension?
options: A record of the sun’s movement across the sky.
A line showing the changing height of the barometer.
A portrait showing a man at several different ages.
A diagram representing a four-dimensional cube.
the-time-machine.evidence: This line I trace with my finger shows the movement of the barometer.

the-time-machine.question: How long did the Time Traveller say it took to make the small model?
options: One month.
One year.
Three years.
Two years.
the-time-machine.evidence: “It took two years to make,” retorted the Time Traveller.

the-time-machine.question: Who physically sent the model Time Machine on its voyage?
options: Filby, after the Time Traveller explained the controls.
The Psychologist, at the Time Traveller’s direction.
The Medical Man, while peering closely at the mechanism.
The Time Traveller, by pressing the white lever himself.
the-time-machine.evidence: it was the Psychologist himself who sent forth the model Time Machine

the-time-machine.question: What was the Time Traveller’s appearance when he returned to dinner the following Thursday?
options: His coat was torn, and his face was covered in soot.
His coat was dusty and dirty, with green smears down the sleeves.
His clothes were wet from the rain, and his hair was neatly combed.
His evening clothes were stained with blood and mud.
the-time-machine.evidence: His coat was dusty and dirty, and smeared with green down the sleeves

the-time-machine.question: What food did the Time Traveller ask the guests to save for him?
options: A bowl of soup.
A piece of roast beef.
Some fruit and bread.
A plate of mutton.
the-time-machine.evidence: Save me some of that mutton.

the-time-machine.question: What happened when the Time Traveller first tried the completed machine?
options: The clock stopped while the room filled with a grey mist.
The laboratory disappeared, and he found himself outside in daylight.
The clock seemed to move from just after ten to nearly half-past three.
The machine moved across the room but did not travel through time.
the-time-machine.evidence: now it was nearly half-past three!

the-time-machine.question: What date did the little dials of the Time Machine show when the Traveller first arrived in the future?
options: The year Eight Hundred and Two Thousand and One.
The year Eight Hundred and Twenty Thousand Seven Hundred and One.
The year Eight Hundred and Two Thousand Seven Hundred and One.
The year Eight Hundred and Two Thousand Seven Hundred and Ten.
the-time-machine.evidence: the date the little dials of my machine recorded.

the-time-machine.question: How did the Time Traveller first meet Weena?
options: He found her asleep in the Palace of Green Porcelain.
He rescued her when she was being carried away by Morlocks.
He pulled her from a river after she was seized with cramp.
He helped her after she fell from the pedestal of the White Sphinx.
the-time-machine.evidence: one of them was seized with cramp and began drifting downstream.

the-time-machine.question: What did the Time Traveller call the disappearance of houses and the apparent communal life of the future people?
options: “Communism.”
“The Great Peace.”
“The perfect conquest of Nature.”
“The Golden Age.”
the-time-machine.evidence: ‘Communism,’ said I to myself.

the-time-machine.question: What did the Time Traveller find on the Morlocks’ table in the underground cavern?
options: What seemed to be a meal, including a red joint of meat.
A box of matches and a piece of camphor.
A collection of tools and small metal parts.
A pile of fruit and a bowl of water.
the-time-machine.evidence: a little table of white metal, laid with what seemed a meal.

the-time-machine.question: What useful items did the Time Traveller find in an airtight case at the Palace of Green Porcelain?
options: A box of matches and a sealed jar of camphor.
A hatchet and a case of gunpowder.
A lamp and a bundle of dry grass.
A set of cartridges and a metal crowbar.
the-time-machine.evidence: I found a box of matches. They were perfectly good.

the-time-machine.question: What happened to the large crab-like creatures in the Traveller’s later glimpse of the far future?
options: They gathered around the Time Machine and attacked it.
They were replaced by flocks of large white flying creatures.
They disappeared, leaving the beach apparently lifeless apart from green growth.
They retreated into the sea as the sun grew brighter.
the-time-machine.evidence: the crawling multitude of crabs had disappeared

the-time-machine.question: How long before the narrator’s account was the Time Traveller said to have vanished?
options: Three years.
Ten years.
Two years.
One year.
the-time-machine.evidence: The Time Traveller vanished three years ago.

the-time-machine.question: Why does the Time Traveller argue that time should be regarded as a fourth dimension?
options: Because mathematical planes and lines have thickness when observed over long periods.
Because all real objects must exist through duration as well as through the three dimensions of space.
Because human consciousness can move freely through time just as the body moves through space.
Because time can be measured only by comparing the lengths of physical objects.
the-time-machine.evidence: any real body must have extension in four directions: it must have Length, Breadth, Thickness, and—Duration.

the-time-machine.question: Why are the guests initially reluctant to believe the Time Traveller’s claims, despite seeing the model vanish?
options: They think he is too clever and possibly concealing a trick behind his frankness.
They believe Filby has secretly arranged the demonstration to deceive them.
They think the Psychologist has hypnotised them during the demonstration.
They suspect the machine is a conventional invention from another country.
the-time-machine.evidence: we distrusted him. Things that would have made the fame of a less clever man seemed tricks in his hands.

the-time-machine.question: What does the Time Traveller’s exhausted, dishevelled return suggest about his journey?
options: It has been a physically dangerous experience, not merely a demonstration or practical joke.
He has spent the journey preparing a story that will win the Editor’s attention.
He has been unable to operate the machine and has spent the week hiding nearby.
He has returned from a brief trip but deliberately altered his appearance to persuade the guests.
the-time-machine.evidence: I’ve lived eight days … such days as no human being ever lived before!

the-time-machine.question: How does the Time Traveller’s view of the Eloi change as he learns more about their world?
options: He begins by thinking they are Morlocks, then learns they are visitors from another planet.
He first fears them as powerful rulers, then discovers they are harmless workers.
He comes to admire their intelligence after initially dismissing their appearance.
He moves from seeing them as evidence of a peaceful paradise to recognizing their weakness and danger.
the-time-machine.evidence: I understood now what all the beauty of the Overworld people covered.

the-time-machine.question: What is the central irony in the Time Traveller’s first explanation of the future society?
options: He believes the future has eliminated nature, but finds that the landscape is entirely barren.
He interprets ease and security as a lasting triumph, but they have helped produce decline and vulnerability.
He expects a world without technology, but discovers that machines control every part of daily life.
He assumes the Eloi have conquered the Morlocks, but learns that the Eloi live underground.
the-time-machine.evidence: Very simple was my explanation, and plausible enough—as most wrong theories are!

the-time-machine.question: What does the division between Eloi and Morlocks suggest about the long-term consequences of social class division?
options: The upper class loses its wealth, while the workers remain unchanged.
The division can become a biological split, with each group adapted to a different way of life.
The workers eventually become rulers because they gain access to education.
The division disappears once the rich and poor share the same buildings.
the-time-machine.evidence: Man had not remained one species, but had differentiated into two distinct animals

the-time-machine.question: Why does the Time Traveller’s rescue of Weena matter to his understanding of the Eloi?
options: It persuades him to abandon his search for the Time Machine permanently.
It proves that Weena can explain the Morlocks’ machinery and underground society.
It convinces him that the Eloi are capable of defending themselves from danger.
It reveals that personal affection and gratitude persist, complicating his view of them as merely mindless creatures.
the-time-machine.evidence: by merely seeming fond of me, and showing in her weak, futile way that she cared for me

the-time-machine.question: What role does Weena’s fear of darkness play in the Traveller’s discoveries?
options: It shows that the Eloi have retained a fear of storms from their ancestors.
It points toward a danger from the Morlocks that the Eloi cannot explain directly.
It leads him to believe that the White Sphinx moves at night.
It makes him realize that the Eloi can see better in darkness than in daylight.
the-time-machine.evidence: It was from her, too, that I learnt that fear had not yet left the world.

the-time-machine.question: Why does the Time Traveller’s theory about the Morlocks and Eloi change after he sees the Morlocks underground?
options: He discovers that the Morlocks are visitors from the past rather than descendants of humanity.
He realizes that the Eloi have deliberately chosen to live underground.
He recognizes that the two groups’ relationship has reversed, and that the Eloi may now be prey.
He learns that the Morlocks are simply the Eloi’s servants and have no independent society.
the-time-machine.evidence: The two species that had resulted from the evolution of man were sliding down towards, or had already arrived at, an altogether new relationship.

the-time-machine.question: What is the significance of the Time Traveller’s loss and recovery of the machine?
options: It teaches him that the Eloi have mastered time travel and can control his machine.
It proves that the machine is destroyed whenever its owner travels far into the future.
It convinces him that the Morlocks are incapable of planning or using tools.
It forces him to rely on observation and adaptation before he can understand how to escape.
the-time-machine.evidence: I had made myself the most complicated and the most hopeless trap that ever a man devised.

the-time-machine.question: Why does the fire in the forest become both a defense and a disaster?
options: It illuminates the path to the White Sphinx, but destroys the Time Machine inside it.
It gives Weena a new way to make fire, but attracts the Eloi to the Morlocks’ tunnels.
It frightens the light-sensitive Morlocks, but spreads through the dry forest and costs the Traveller Weena.
It drives the Morlocks underground, but leaves the Traveller without any matches.
the-time-machine.evidence: It was my first fire coming after me. With that I looked for Weena, but she was gone.

the-time-machine.question: What broader idea does the Traveller draw from the decline of both the Eloi and the Morlocks?
options: A society becomes stable only when one group completely defeats another.
Humanity’s future depends mainly on preserving its ancient buildings and artifacts.
Comfort and specialization can weaken capacities that once helped people respond to change and danger.
Technological progress always improves intelligence, even when people stop working.
the-time-machine.evidence: There is no intelligence where there is no change and no need of change.

the-time-machine.question: Why is the Time Traveller’s later journey to the dying Earth important to the work’s view of human progress?
options: It shows that the Morlocks eventually build a civilization more advanced than the present one.
It places human history within a much larger cosmic future in which Earth itself becomes desolate.
It proves that the Traveller’s machine can move through space but not through time.
It confirms that humanity will return to the same social arrangement seen among the Eloi.
the-time-machine.evidence: watching with a strange fascination the sun grow larger and duller in the westward sky, and the life of the old earth ebb away.

the-time-machine.question: What do the withered flowers from Weena ultimately represent to the narrator?
options: Proof that the Time Traveller’s story was fabricated from specimens in a museum.
A warning that the Eloi’s gardens will soon be destroyed by the Morlocks.
Evidence that tenderness and gratitude can survive even after much of humanity’s strength and intelligence have vanished.
A reminder that the Time Traveller’s machine cannot return to the present.
the-time-machine.evidence: gratitude and a mutual tenderness still lived on in the heart of man.

the-time-machine.question: How does the ending preserve uncertainty about the Time Traveller’s final fate?
options: He returns from the future with photographs that prove every part of his account.
He is found dead in the laboratory after the machine breaks apart.
He tells the narrator exactly which historical era he intends to visit next.
He disappears on another journey, and the narrator can only speculate about where he went.
the-time-machine.evidence: The Time Traveller vanished three years ago. And, as everybody knows now, he has never returned.
